1:
The name of the feast is disputed before anything else. Bede denies the common derivation: Pascha, in Hebrew phase, is not named from Passion as many think but from passing over, because the destroyer, seeing the blood on the Israelites’ doors, passed by without smiting them — or because the Lord himself, bringing aid to his people, walked above them. He distinguishes the two feasts: the day alone on which the lamb was slain, the fourteenth moon of the first month, was called Passover, while the feast of unleavened bread came on at the fifteenth, when they came out of Egypt. Pseudo-Jerome allows that sense for phase but says Pascha means sacrifice, and opens the chapter as liturgy rather than commentary: let us sprinkle our book and our thresholds with blood, put the scarlet thread about the house of our prayers and bind scarlet on our hand, that we may say the red heifer is slain in the valley — for the Evangelist, about to speak of the slaying of Christ, premises the two days before the Passover. Robertson takes the phrase as covering both names and the whole eight days, and Barnes explains the second, that at that feast no bread was used but what had been made without leaven.

The date is worked out with some care. Robertson makes it Tuesday evening as we count, the beginning of the Jewish Wednesday, notes that Matthew reports Jesus naming the same date, which would put it at our Thursday evening, and that John mentions five items which superficially seem to contradict this but are really in harmony. Gill fixes it by what precedes: two days after Christ had delivered the discourse about the destruction of the temple; the feast itself commemorated God’s passing over the houses of the Israelites when he destroyed the firstborn of Egypt.

Theophylact adds the line that reverses the direction of the scene: whatever the priests were contriving, Christ himself had determined the day of his Passion, wishing to be crucified at the Passover because he was the true Passover. Henry reaches the same conclusion from the other end, with two reasons why he must be crucified at that feast: that his death might be the more public, so that all Israel, even those of the dispersion, might be witnesses; and that the antitype might answer to the type, Christ our Passover being sacrificed at the very time the paschal lamb was sacrificed and the deliverance from Egypt commemorated.

On the plot itself the comments divide between malice and calculation. Henry marks how spiteful they were, not thinking it enough to banish or imprison him but aiming to be revenged for all the good he had done; and how subtle, since their stated reason for delay is not that the people would be diverted from their devotions but that there might be an uproar — men who desired nothing more than the praise of men dreading nothing more than their rage. Barnes glosses the craft as subtilty, some secret plan that would secure possession of him without exciting the opposition of the people. Gill explains the crowd they feared as the concourse gathering from all parts to keep the feast. Robertson reconstructs the change of mind: they had first planned to kill him at the feast, and it was the Triumphal Entry and the great debate in the temple that very morning which made them decide to wait until it was over, since it had become plain that Jesus had too large and powerful a following.
3:
The chain reads the setting allegorically, the rest topographically. Bede finds it fitting that the Lord, about to suffer for the world, should dwell at Bethany, the house of obedience, and explains the host’s name: Simon is called the leper not because he was still one but because, having once been such, he had been healed. Pseudo-Jerome makes Simon the leper the world, at first unbelieving and afterwards converted, and the woman with the box the faith of the Church, whose spikenard sends forth its smell; the nard is called pistic, faithful and precious. Gill supplies the plain account: Bethany lay two miles from Jerusalem, and Christ retired there after taking leave of the temple, going to and fro often that last week because he had dear friends in the place.

How many anointings there were is the open question. Theophylact answers that though all four Evangelists record an anointing there were two women and not one, John describing the sister of Lazarus and the other three another — then revises himself, that on examination one finds three, one in John, another in Luke, a third in the remaining two. Augustine takes the opposite view, that the sinner who came to Jesus’s feet was the same Mary who did this twice, once as Luke relates when she came with humility and tears and merited remission. Robertson settles only that this differs from the incident in Luke.

The ointment and its price occupy the moderns. Barnes objects to the English word, since this was a liquid perfume used only to give a pleasant odour, and describes the nard as an East Indian plant with a slender stalk and a heavy thick root, the best perfume coming from the root. Clarke canvasses the alabaster box — a glass phial, a small vessel without a handle, or an essence bottle — and reports that many manuscripts add the word for the ointment in the next verse. Lightfoot works from Pliny, giving the composition of nardine and the market prices of such ointments, which he says were commonly known. Robertson notes the adjective joined to the nard occurs only here and in John, and that the verb for murmuring is used of the snorting of horses. On the sum, Gill gives nine pounds seven shillings and sixpence, Clarke nearly ten pounds, Barnes about forty-one dollars; Ellicott notes the figure, absent from Matthew, is one of the few points common to Mark and John, and Robertson that the “far above” may come from Peter’s memory of the objection.

On the objectors and the defence the witnesses are careful. Ellicott notes Mark limits the murmurers to some, an intermediate stage between Matthew’s disciples and John’s naming of Judas; Wesley that they were incited by Judas and probably spoke to the women. Origen states the complaint and answers it: they were grieved at the waste, which might have been sold and given to the poor, but this ought not to have been, since it was right that the ointment should be poured over the head of Christ. Ellicott glosses the word for the good work as noble, the higher form of goodness, and peculiar to Mark. Gill has Christ, knowing their indignation and their continual teasing of the woman, tell them to cease chiding her. Henry reads it as a double kindness, one friend inviting him to supper and Christ accepting though his death was near, another pouring all the ointment on his head — and since alabaster is not easily broken, he records the reading that she shook or struck the box rather than shattering it. On the burial he observes that those condemned to die commonly have their coffins prepared while still alive, and that Christ accepted this in the same spirit; he never rode in triumph into Jerusalem but when he came to suffer, nor had his head anointed but for his burial.
10:
The motive is supplied from what precedes. Bede has Judas seeking to make good with the price of his Master the loss he reckoned he had suffered by the pouring out of the ointment, and Wesley says he went immediately after the reproof, with anger now added to his covetousness; Gill notes that he was the principal person who had taken indignation at the woman. Bede also presses the words “he went”, which show that he was neither invited by the chief priests nor bound by any necessity but entered on the design from the spontaneous wickedness of his own mind — and observes that many who shudder at the crime as monstrous do not take heed to themselves. Henry adds the practical question of what Judas had to offer: he proposed to give them notice when and where they might seize Christ without an uproar among the people, though it is unlikely he knew where their counsels had run aground, since that debate was held in their close cabal, or that they knew any of his intimates would stoop so low — but Satan, who had entered into Judas, knew what occasion they had for him.

The phrase “one of the twelve” is weighed by several. Chrysostom takes it as aggravating the guilt, since there were seventy other disciples not admitted to such familiar intercourse, and notes two things about the naming: that the surname is given to distinguish this Judas from the other of that name, the brother of James, and that the Evangelist does not write “Judas the traitor”, so teaching us to be guiltless of detraction and to avoid accusing others — though he adds, of the man himself, that he would he could have been ignorant of his existence. Pseudo-Jerome sharpens it to an epigram: he was one of the twelve in number, not in merit, one in body, not in soul. Robertson notes the article, which Matthew lacks, and rejects the suggestion some have made that Mark is calling Judas the primate among the twelve; the point is rather that he was the one of the twelve who did this deed.

The bargain draws short and severe comment. Pseudo-Jerome finds a likeness between the parties, since Judas went to the chief priests after Satan had entered into him and every living thing unites with what is like itself, and reads his promise as an echo of the devil’s own offer of all this power; the priests promise money and lose their life, which he too loses on receiving it, and no opportunity for treachery can be found that escapes vengeance here or hereafter. Clarke says flatly that joy arising from the opportunity of murdering an innocent person must be completely infernal. Gill explains what pleased them, that the offer came from one of Christ’s own disciples, so that the thing might be done more secretly and effectually and with less blame to themselves; Theophylact that betraying him meant announcing when he should be alone, since they feared to rush upon him while he was teaching. Ellicott adds two observations from comparison: the mention of the priests being glad is shared with Luke, and Mark does not name the specific sum promised as the price of blood.
12:
The date is contested. Bede takes the first day of the Passover for the fourteenth of the first month, when leaven was thrown aside and the lamb killed at even, and holds that although Christ was crucified on the fifteenth moon, it was on the night the lamb was offered that he acted — citing the apostle that Christ our Passover is sacrificed for us. Robertson describes the same practice grammatically, the imperfect marking customary observance: the lamb was slain at six in the evening, beginning the fifteenth, while preparations were made beforehand on the fourteenth. Gill simply identifies the day as the fourteenth of Nisan. Lightfoot puts the difficulty as a challenge: those who hold that Christ kept his Passover on the fourteenth while the Jews deferred theirs to the fifteenth, on account of the following sabbath, must say whether the evangelists speak by the day Moses prescribed or by the day then observed.

The arrangements are read for what they show about Christ. Chrysostom sets the scene against the previous one: while Judas was plotting the betrayal, the rest of the disciples were busy about the preparation — not of our Passover but, for the present, that of the Jews. Theophylact infers from the disciples’ question that Christ had no dwelling-place and they no houses of their own, since otherwise they would have taken him there; and from the sending of two disciples to a man unknown to them, that Christ might, had he pleased, have avoided his Passion. Pseudo-Jerome takes the same question as a lesson, that we should direct our steps by the will of God, and reads the unleavened bread eaten with bitter herbs as our redemption, the bitterness being the Passion. Henry attends to Christ’s composure, observing that he prepared for approaching sorrows with the joys of this ordinance, the full prospect of what was coming not indisposing him for the solemnity — from which he draws the rule that no apprehension of trouble should put us out of frame for holy ordinances.

The sign of the water-carrier draws the most comment, and the witnesses differ over what it proves. Clarke exclaims at the exactness of the foreknowledge, which comprehends the minutest circumstances, and turns it into a doctrine of providence: an honest employment, however mean, is worthy of God’s attention, and even a man bearing a pitcher of water is marked in all his steps. Wesley makes it seasonable rather than exemplary, an additional proof given just when it was needed both of Christ knowing all things and of his influence over the minds of men. Theophylact, as above, makes the same detail evidence that the Passion was voluntary.

The remaining notes are comparative. Ellicott observes that the number of the messengers is given by Mark and their names, Peter and John, by Luke only, and that the sign of the pitcher is common to Mark and Luke but absent from Matthew; Robertson says the same of both details, and Gill names the two disciples from the parallel. Augustine reconciles a small discrepancy between the accounts, that where Mark says a pitcher Luke says a two-handed vessel — the one pointing out the kind of vessel and the other the mode of carrying it, both meaning the same truth. Barnes explains what preparing the Passover involved, namely to procure a lamb, have it roasted and properly furnished with the usual accompaniments, and notes that the city meant is Jerusalem, the party being then at Bethany about two miles off. Pseudo-Jerome adds only that the Lord points out with whom he would eat, and that he sends two disciples after his custom.
17:
Why the warning is given at all, and in that form, is the first question. Bede holds that the Lord, having foretold his Passion, prophesied also of the traitor in order to give him room for repentance, so that understanding his thoughts were known he might repent; and he identifies the man by his conduct, since Judas, when the others were sad and held back their hands, put his hand into the dish with his Master. Chrysostom explains the balance struck: Christ did not proclaim him openly to all, lest he should make him the more shameless, and yet did not keep silent altogether, lest thinking himself undiscovered he should hasten the more boldly to the betrayal. Theophylact accounts for the disciples’ sorrow by their distrust of themselves — although they were free of this passion, they trusted him who knows all hearts rather than their own knowledge — and Gill notes that all were sorrowful except Judas.

The posture at table is disputed on two different grounds. Theophylact raises it as a question of law: how could they eat reclining, when the law ordered that the Passover be eaten standing and upright? His answer is that they had probably fulfilled the legal Passover first, and had reclined when Christ began to give them his own. Ellicott and Robertson raise it as a question of translation, Ellicott correcting “as they sat” to “as they reclined” and Robertson calling it a pity that these verbs are not properly rendered in English — observing that even Leonardo da Vinci, in his painting of the Last Supper, has Jesus and the apostles sitting rather than reclining, probably by an artist’s licence for effect. Gill gives the same correction more briefly, that the phrase means as they lay along, such being the posture at the Passover.

Robertson also draws out the force of eating together, noting that to this day the Arabs will not violate hospitality by mistreating one who has broken bread with them in the tent; and he places the meal at the regular hour, six in the evening at the beginning of the fifteenth. Gill reconstructs the day’s movements, that Christ set out from Bethany in the afternoon with the nine, was joined at Jerusalem by Judas and by the two who had gone ahead, and went with all twelve to the house when the second evening had come. Pseudo-Jerome reads the hour figuratively instead, the evening of the day pointing to the evening of the world, when the last, who are first to receive the penny of eternal life, come about the eleventh hour; and he turns the disciples’ questioning into an image of a harp, all the well-attuned strings answering with accordant tone, with one alone unstrung and steeped in the love of money. Clarke supplies a textual note on that questioning, that the clause reporting a second speaker is wanting in many manuscripts and versions, Griesbach leaving it doubtful and others omitting it.

On the last verse the emphasis falls on the willingness of the sufferer. Cyril of Jerusalem asks whether one would be persuaded that Christ came to his passion willingly, and answers from the foreknowledge: others, who do not foresee it, die unwillingly, whereas he spoke of his passion beforehand, saying that the Son of man is betrayed to be crucified — and the question that follows is why this Friend of man did not shun the death he saw coming.
22:
Bede marks the transition: when the rites of the old Passover were finished the Lord passed to the new, substituting the sacrament of his own Body and Blood for the flesh and blood of the lamb, and taking bread to show that he is the one to whom it was sworn, Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedec. Gill places the moment exactly, at the conclusion of the paschal lamb and the unleavened bread. Henry states the character of the ordinance rather than its metaphysics: the supper is food for the soul, so a very little of what is for the body — as much as will serve for a sign — is enough; it was instituted by our Master’s example to remain in force till his second coming, with blessing and giving of thanks, as a memorial of his death.

What the bread becomes is the chapter’s sharpest division. Theophylact denies it is a mere figure of the Body and holds that it is changed into the very Body, since the Lord said the bread he gives is his flesh — that flesh being veiled from our eyes on account of our weakness. Chrysostom locates the agency rather than the substance: Christ, who prepared that table, himself consecrates it, and it is not man who makes the offerings to be the Body and Blood but Christ who was crucified for us, the words being spoken by the priest’s mouth and consecrated by the power of God. Cyril of Jerusalem appeals to Paul’s account of the night of the betrayal as itself sufficient assurance concerning the divine mysteries, by which those deemed worthy become of the same body and blood with Christ. Calvin turns the whole toward the death: the words direct us to the sacrifice of Christ’s death, without the remembrance of which the Supper is never rightly observed, since believing souls cannot be satisfied otherwise than by being assured that God is pacified toward them. Pseudo-Jerome takes a third course, reading the bread mystically as the Church itself, received in faith, blessed in its number, broken in its sufferings, given in its examples and taken in its doctrines, while the Blood is formed in a chalice of water and wine mingled.

Gregory attends to a detail the others pass over, that Christ gave thanks with the Passion approaching. He who took on him the stripes of other men’s wickedness, having done nothing worthy of smiting, humbly gave a blessing in his suffering — showing what each should do when beaten for his own sins, since Christ bore calmly the stripes due to others’ sin.

The remaining notes are textual and comparative. Clarke reports that the word for eating is omitted by many manuscripts and versions but thinks it should stand, since it is found in the parallel passages. Ellicott observes that Mark agrees with Matthew in using blessing of the bread and giving thanks of the cup, whereas Luke uses the second of the bread and implies by his likewise that the form was repeated over the cup; and he corrects the tense of the clause about the blood, the participle being present. Gill notes the thanks were given over the cup and for it, appropriating it to the present service, and that the words about the blood were spoken as Christ gave the cup rather than after they had drunk. Robertson takes the cup to have held the ordinary wine of the country mixed with two parts water, and observes that the word for wine is not used here at all but the fruit of the vine; Mark and Matthew give substantially the same account, while Luke agrees closely with Paul’s.
26:
The hymn is identified three different ways. Gill names it the Hallel used at the Passover. Bede suggests instead that it may be the hymn recorded in John, which the Lord sang in returning thanks to the Father, praying with raised eyes for himself, for his disciples, and for those who should believe through their word. Lightfoot approaches it through rabbinic law, citing the distinction between the first Passover and the second: in the first a man is bound under the rule that leaven shall not be seen with him, and bound also to a hymn when he eats the Passover, whereas in the second leaven and unleavened bread may both be in his house. Theophylact draws a rule of practice from the placing of it: as they gave thanks before they drank, so after, which teaches us to give thanks both before and after our food — and he finds in the singing evidence that Christ was glad to die for us, since when about to be betrayed he deigned to praise God. Pseudo-Jerome takes the hymn as the praise of the Lord, quoting the psalm that the poor shall eat and be satisfied.

The place is read typologically. Bede finds it fitting that the Lord should lead his disciples to the mount of Olives when they had tasted his sacraments, to show that through them we ought to rise to higher gifts of virtue. Pseudo-Jerome notes that Jesus is held captive on the mount from which he ascended, so that we may know we ascend to heaven from the place where we watch and pray. Calvin observes what the passage omits: the three Evangelists leave out the discourses John reports as delivered in the house and on the road, since their object was the history of our Lord’s actions rather than his doctrine, and they glance only at his going out of his own accord to where Judas would come.

The prediction of the denial raises a harmonising difficulty which Augustine alone confronts. All the Evangelists say the Lord foretold that Peter would deny him before the cock crew, but Mark alone relates the matter more minutely, and some from inattention suppose him to disagree with the rest. Augustine’s answer turns on the denial being threefold: had the whole of it begun only after the cock crew, the other three would seem to have spoken falsely in saying he would deny thrice before it. Wesley handles a different part of the same verse, explaining that the Jews reckoned their days from the evening, according to the Mosaic computation which calls the evening and the morning the first day, so that what after sunset is called here this night is in the next verse called this day — and he draws out the force of the accumulation, that Peter, confident as he was, would fail today, within four and twenty hours, indeed this very night. Clarke presses the same emphasis from the text, noting that the pronoun for “thou” is added by a great many manuscripts and versions and adds much to the energy of a passage in which every word is deeply emphatical. Ellicott takes up the other disputed word, that “twice” is omitted in many manuscripts but agrees with the emphatic mention of a second cockcrow later in the chapter and with the form of the prediction there, so that it may fairly be regarded as the true reading and the omission accidental; on Peter’s reply he notes that the Greek tense implies frequent and continuous speaking.

Gill follows the exchange clause by clause: Christ spoke as they went to the mount; he assures them of his rising for their comfort, though they would be discouraged by his seizing and condemnation; and Peter answers as one greatly moved at being told that all would be offended that night and scattered.
32:
The place is expounded before the prayer. Gloss introduces the scene as the account of a prayer supposed to have been offered for the disciples, the place being described first. Bede reports that Gethsemane is still shown at the foot of the Mount of Olives and gives its meaning as the valley of fatness, drawing a contrast: praying on a mountain teaches us to ask for lofty things, praying in the valley of fatness that humility and the fatness of interior love must be kept. Gill explains the name from the trade, where the olives of the mount were pressed, adding that there our Lord began to be bruised for our sins. Pseudo-Jerome hears the psalm in the same word, that in the valley of fatness the fat bulls beset him, and finds a figure in the parting: they are separated from him in prayer who are separated from him in his Passion, for he prays while they sleep.

The choice of the three is read as deliberate. Theophylact notes it was Christ’s custom always to pray by himself, giving us an example of silence and solitude in prayer, and that he took only those who had witnessed his glory on Tabor, so that they might see his sufferings too and learn from his sorrow that he is really man. Henry states what the agony was: Christ begins his sufferings with the sorest of them, those in his soul, and this agony was the wormwood and the gall of the whole affliction — showing that no sorrow was forced on him but that he freely admitted it. On the word for his distress, Ellicott notes Mark uses a stronger term than Matthew’s; Robertson that Mark alone uses it, its cognate having described the disciples’ amazement at the look of Jesus as he went toward Jerusalem, so that now Jesus himself feels amazement; Wesley that the original imports the most shocking amazement mingled with grief, the next word intimating that he was surrounded with sorrow on every side, breaking in with such violence as was ready to separate soul from body.

The single Aramaic word draws six of the witnesses. Ellicott notes the record of Abba as actually uttered is peculiar to Mark, with possible traces of the impression it made in Romans and Galatians. Robertson denies it is translation at all, both terms standing together with the article on each as in Galatians, and suggests a memory of Paul’s childhood prayers. Wesley thinks Mark adds the Greek word by way of explication. Gill takes the doubling either as explanation or as expressing the vehemence of Christ’s affection and his confidence in God as Father amid his distress. Barnes and Clarke gloss it as a term of filial affection and tenderness, Clarke adding that it seems used by our Lord merely as man, showing his complete submission to his Father’s will. Lightfoot distinguishes the idioms, the Hebrew form signifying a civil father as well as a natural one — an elder, a master, a magistrate — whereas the other denotes the natural relation only. Augustine takes up the condition: Christ said not if he could do it but if it could be done, since whatever he wills is possible, so the condition means if he is willing — and lest anyone suppose the Father’s power lessened, the next words declare that all things are possible to him.

On the sleeping disciples the notes are brief and pointed. Ellicott observes that where Matthew and Luke give the question in the plural Mark reports it in the singular and joins it to the emphatic naming of the disciple, including both questions that appear separately elsewhere. Robertson marks which name is used — the old one, not the new — and says that Peter’s boasted loyalty was already failing in the hour of crisis; Wesley calls him the zealous, the confident Peter.
43:
The betrayer’s approach is read for what it shows of him. Bede has the Lord, having prayed three times and obtained that the apostles’ fear should be amended by later repentance, go tranquil to his persecutors; and he finds Judas retained something of a disciple’s shame. Theophylact says the description “one of the twelve” is not added without reason but to the greater conviction of the traitor, since a man of the chief company turned himself to furious enmity; and he marks the blindness of one who thought to deceive Christ by a kiss. Pseudo-Jerome states the principle behind the crowd: he who despairs of help from God has recourse to the power of the world — and he sets the kiss beside Cain’s crafty and reprobate sacrifice, calling Christ the Joseph sold by his brethren into whose soul the iron entered. Henry observes that this was what the enemies had long aimed at and often attempted, but that they could not have taken him now had he not freely surrendered himself, having begun to suffer first in his soul.

The arrangements are noted precisely. Robertson observes that Mark adds the scribes where John mentions Pharisees, and that this was evidently a committee of the Sanhedrin, since Judas had made his bargain with that body; he calls the agreed-on signal a word common in ancient Greek but found only here in the New Testament, and notes that the instruction to lead him away safely is peculiar to Mark, Judas wishing no slip to occur. Gill says the same, that it was a common sign in which they had agreed. Ellicott corrects the rendering of the order: it means seize, not merely take. Wesley suggests that our Lord in great condescension had permitted his disciples, after the Jewish custom, to greet him so when they had been some time absent.

The young man who fled is the passage’s puzzle, and the witnesses divide widely. Robertson reports the usual supposition that it was Mark himself, son of the Mary in whose house they had probably kept the passover, and calls the detail a lifelike touch; Ellicott notes that the incident is narrated by Mark alone, that it had clearly made a deep impression on some of the disciples, and that although some have supposed it was Mark there is no ground for it. Calvin is blunter about a rival guess: he does not know how some have come to dream that it was John, nor does he think it of much importance to inquire — the chief point being why Mark related it at all, which he takes to be to show how those wicked men stormed as men do in riotous assemblies. Gregory, by contrast, states the identification with John as a fact. Gill lists the candidates — John, James the Lord’s brother, a young man of the house where they had eaten the passover — and concludes he was not a disciple at all, since he is distinguished from those who all fled. Barnes agrees he was not an apostle, supposes him roused from sleep in some neighbouring house by the noise, and admits it is not known why Mark records it; Clarke and Wesley tell the same story of a sleeper who caught up his bed-clothes and ran out to see what was happening. Lightfoot cuts against that whole reconstruction from the Talmudists: the word means clothed in fine linen, and implies not that some cloth had been loosely and by chance cast about him but that the garment he always went clothed in was of linen.

Two further notes close the arrest. Gill compares the leaving of the cloth to Joseph leaving his garment in his mistress’s hands. Wesley draws the contrast that the officers laid hold on one who was only suspected of being a disciple, and yet could not touch those who really were.
53:
The transfer to the ecclesiastical court is marked. The Gloss notes the seam: the evangelist has told how the Lord was taken, and now begins how he was condemned to death in the high priest’s house. Gill names Caiaphas from the Syriac, Arabic and Persic versions, and places this after Annas. Bede identifies him from John as high priest that year, bought (says Josephus) from the Roman Emperor. Theophylact uses the same fact to explain the plural: the law commanded one high priest, but men were put into the office and stripped of it year by year, so that those called chief priests are those whose time had run out. Henry observes the state Caiaphas kept, that in the dead of night all who were in the secret were assembled and ready to receive the prey, and that the judge had lately adjudged this man’s death expedient and was thus plainly partial.

Peter’s position is described in the same detail. Bede finds it fitting that the man about to deny follows afar off, since he could not have denied Christ had he stayed close; Pseudo-Jerome puts it the other way, that fear holds him back while love draws him on. Henry sees his late courage dwindled into cowardice, and calls the sitting down with servants his entrance into the temptation. Gill has another disciple, perhaps John, go in with Jesus and Peter admitted by his means. Robertson notes that Mark uses a plain aorist where Matthew and Luke have the picturesque imperfect; that the periphrastic imperfect shows Peter making himself at home with the officers, literally under-rowers; and that since John has him standing, he probably did now one and now the other in his restless weary mood.

The fire is read two ways, and the division is sharp. Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson keep to the physical fact: the phrase is literally at the light, and the glare of the charcoal on Peter’s face is why the servant girl could distinguish him — he was not hidden as much as he supposed. Bede and Pseudo-Jerome take it as a figure. Bede grants that charity is a fire, but covetousness is one also, and that this fire, raised in the hall by an evil spirit, armed the traitors’ tongues and figured what the assembly was doing within, since where iniquity abounds the love of many waxes cold; Peter, benumbed by that cold, warmed himself at the coals of Caiaphas’s servants because he sought worldly comfort among traitors. Pseudo-Jerome reads the hall as the world, the servants as devils among whom no man can weep for his sins, and the fire as the desire of the flesh.

On the failure of the evidence the witnesses converge. Henry has them seize a man against whom they had no indictment, then seek witnesses by ensnaring questions, bribes and threats, and notes that the men charged by law with punishing false witnesses were ringleaders in the crime. Wesley calls it an amazing proof of overruling providence that with all their authority and rewards no two consistent witnesses could be got; he and Gill gloss the word as not equal, not answerable to a capital charge. Robertson adds that no two bore joint testimony as the law required, and that the imperfect tenses mark repeated failures. Ellicott notes that Mark alone states the cause Matthew merely implies, and that the made-with-hands antithesis is Mark’s own. Bede defines the fault: a false witness takes words in a sense in which they were not spoken; Pseudo-Jerome says heretics extract the shadow out of the truth. Lightfoot alone brings the court’s own canons, which graded testimony as vain, standing, or agreeing, and observes that had that scrutiny been used, nothing could have been fastened on Christ. Wesley closes by noting that they had to reach back three years for the saying — itself a silent attestation to his conduct.
60:
The silence is explained before it is broken. Bede has the high priest, finding no room for accusation, provoke him so as to catch at anything he said, and rise from his seat, his bodily motion showing the madness of his mind. Gill explains what standing in the midst meant, the president sitting at the head with the council ranged before him. On the silence Gill says a reply would have been to no purpose and the charges unworthy of an answer; Theophylact that he knew they would not attend; Pseudo-Jerome that he was led as a sheep to the slaughter, his silence being the pardon for Adam’s excuse; Henry that it was an example of patience and of prudence, since it is an evil time when a man is made an offender for a word.

The question turns on a title. Theophylact says the high priest asked not to learn but to seek occasion, and chose that form because many were called christs — kings and priests are anointed — but none the Son of the Ever-praised. Clarke notes that manuscripts and versions add the word God, which might be printed in italics, though the adjective stands well alone on a Hebrew idiom. Theophylact alone says why Jesus answered at all: lest they should afterwards claim they had heard nothing, their condemnation being that they heard and did not believe. Augustine makes the answer equivalent to Matthew’s “Thou hast said”; Robertson allows this but calls Mark’s form definite beyond controversy, and notes that Mark drops the adjuration. Henry observes that for proof of his sonship Christ binds them over to his second coming, and marvels that a word of such majesty did not arrest judgment. Cyril of Jerusalem leaves the trial aside and takes the saying as a proof text, marshalling Peter, Romans and Ephesians on the session at the right hand. Augustine adds that the Lord suffered until morning in that house.

The rending of the clothes divides them three ways. Gill and Theophylact treat it as custom, the usual act on hearing blasphemy — which Gill says Caiaphas supposed or would have so thought, and which Theophylact says the Jews used at anything intolerable. Ellicott adds that Mark names the inner garment where Matthew names the outer. Henry and Bede make it a figure: Henry that as Saul’s rending of Samuel’s mantle signified the kingdom rent from him, so this signified the priesthood rent from Caiaphas, Christ’s own clothes being kept entire even at the crucifixion because his priesthood is unchangeable; Bede that the Jewish priest rent his own ephod while the Lord’s garment could not be rent even by the soldiers. Leo alone makes it an offence: Caiaphas, not knowing what his frantic action meant, deprived himself of the priesthood, forgetting the command that the high priest shall not rend his clothes. On the verdict Henry notes the question was prejudged, the president voting first who ought to have voted last; Robertson takes “they all” to imply Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus were absent.

The abuse is described, then read. Henry is struck that priests who had just condemned him helped their servants make sport of the prisoner while waiting for morning. Ellicott points out that the covering of the face, in Mark and Luke but not Matthew, gave the taunt its point: they blindfolded the Prophet and then called on him to see. Robertson adds that the officers are those who still held him, and that the verb first meant to smite with a rod, later to slap with the palm. Bede takes the taunt as aimed at his prophetic claim; Pseudo-Jerome turns each indignity into its remedy: the spitting washed the face of our soul, the covering took the veil from our hearts, the buffets healed the head of mankind in Adam, and the blows earned the praise our clapping hands testify.
66:
The setting is fixed first. Gill places Peter in the lower part of the hall, the sanhedrim’s floor being raised with steps up to it. Henry traces the fall to its beginning, in following afar off and then sitting among the servants, and warns that company with Christ’s disciples is less dangerous than company with his enemies; the temptation he weighs as slight, only a maid casually casting her eye on him. Bede asks why a woman recognised him first when men were better able, and answers that the sex which sinned in the Lord’s death might be redeemed by his Passion. Pseudo-Jerome contrasts the Peter who lost courage at a girl’s voice without the Spirit with the Peter who with it feared no kings, and reads the three challengers as stages of one sin — the first maid the wavering, the second the assent, the third man the act. Theophylact makes it providence, permitted lest Peter be elated and that he might prove merciful to sinners, knowing weakness from himself.

The four accounts are then harmonised. Augustine sets out the orders: Luke puts the temptation before the injuries, John begins it, breaks off, then returns to it, while Matthew and Mark reverse them. He holds the second maid to be another, finds two people addressing Peter there, and argues that Peter had come back to the fire, so that the denial was made within the palace, not before the porch. Gill reports the versions divided, the Syriac and Persic reading “that maid,” the Arabic another, the Ethiopic a daughter of the high priest; Ellicott prefers “the maid,” the one who had pointed him out before. Robertson admits the three denials cannot be related clearly, since several may have joined in each time, both maids and men; Mark’s “the Nazarene” is Matthew’s “the Galilean.”

Two clauses are doubted on manuscript grounds. Robertson reports that the crowing at the first denial is omitted by weighty witnesses and secure only at the second, so that it may have crept in from there; Ellicott judges similarly of the clause about Peter’s speech, wanting in many of the best manuscripts and possibly an interpretative addition by Mark himself in a revised edition. On the accent Bede denies that the Galilaeans spoke a different tongue, both being Hebrews, putting it down to provincial peculiarities; Henry says the same plainly, that they knew him by his speaking broad. Robertson notes that the word for the porch occurs only here in the New Testament, Plato using it of a prelude on a flute; Ellicott glosses it as the space before the palace.

The last word of the chapter is the most disputed. Ellicott takes it literally as throwing at or on, and judges the English rendering right, since to reflect is to bend the mind. Robertson agrees that the idiom supplies the mind, cites a papyrus where the word means to set to, and marks Mark’s imperfect “began to weep” against Matthew’s aorist “burst into tears.” Clarke reports Wakefield’s “he fell a weeping” as nearest, with the guesses of a head wrapped for shame or a hurried exit driven by remorse, and concludes our own translation is as good as any. Henry canvasses more still — he added to weep, continued weeping, threw himself down, covered his face, cast his eyes on his Master — and offers his own, that Peter laid a load upon himself. Wesley takes the covered head for the mourner’s custom, expressing grief and shame. Two lessons close the account, and they pull opposite ways. Theophylact turns the fall into comfort against the Novatians, who deny remission to one who sins after baptism, since Peter, who had received the Body and Blood, is received by penitence; Bede draws the harder lesson, that not only he denies Christ who says he is not the Christ, but the Christian who denies himself to be one.
